planting.note: Plant in early spring into moist, acidic, well-drained soil and mulch to keep roots cool through summer.

directions: This selection was chosen for its consistently powdery, blue-white new growth, which is more pronounced than typical seed-grown honeycup. Site it in acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture, similar to companion bog and pondside shrubs like fetterbush or leucothoe. Light dappled shade brings out the best foliage color while protecting leaves from summer scorch. Prune lightly right after the anise-scented spring flowers fade, since blooms form on old wood.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Transplant container-grown stock in early spring into humus-rich soil on a shaded slope or streambank.

directions: Discovered in 1992 along the McCloud River in Shasta County, California, this suckering deciduous shrub is one of botany's more dramatic rediscoveries of a nearly-lost lineage related to Alabama snow-wreath. It thrives on shaded limestone slopes and streambanks, spreading by root suckers to form loose colonies. Give it consistent moisture and dappled to full shade, echoing its native canyon habitat, and allow room for it to naturalize rather than confining it to a tight bed. Frothy white spring flowers lack petals but have showy stamen tufts that resemble small white pom-poms.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in spring or fall into average, well-drained soil.

directions: Bred in the Netherlands from Symphoricarpos x doorenbosii crosses, 'Marleen' stays noticeably more compact and heavily fruited than the older species types, making it useful for foundation plantings or mixed shrub borders in dry shade. It tolerates poor, rocky, or clay soils and shrugs off root competition beneath established trees. The dense clusters of rose-pink berries persist into winter and are a valuable food source for birds. Cut back hard every few years to renew flowering and fruiting wood.

planting.note: Space plants for a continuous informal hedge and plant in spring or fall in ordinary garden soil.

directions: This upright, densely twiggy selection was developed for hedging and screening in tough urban or woodland-edge sites where little else will grow in dry shade. It produces abundant chalky-white berries in fall that hold well into winter, brightening shaded borders after leaves drop. Established plants tolerate heavy shade, road salt, and poor soil, and can be sheared once after fruiting to maintain a tidy hedge form. Suckering habit makes it useful for stabilizing shaded slopes as well.

planting.note: Plant in spring on slopes or beneath trees where a low, spreading groundcover shrub is needed.

directions: A natural hybrid between coralberry and creeping snowberry, 'Hancock' forms a low, dense, arching groundcover rather than an upright shrub, rooting where trailing stems touch soil. It is prized for erosion control on shaded banks and under mature trees where turf fails, tolerating dry shade, root competition, and poor soil once established. Small pinkish summer flowers give way to sparse coral-pink berries partly hidden by the foliage. An occasional hard mow or shear in late winter keeps growth dense and prevents woody buildup.
